hacker_news.title: Taking over US Treasury subdomains for $3 each
hacker_news.author: negura
hacker_news.summary: We took over five US Treasury subdomains for about $3 each by cycling through AWS Elastic IPs. Here’s how it works, and what to check in your own DNS.

linked_context.page_title: Taking over US Treasury subdomains for $3 each
linked_context.page_description: We took over five US Treasury subdomains for about $3 each by cycling through AWS Elastic IPs. Here’s how it works, and what to check in your own DNS.
linked_context.page_excerpt:
Elastic IP addresses (EIPs) in AWS are internet routable addresses available for use on cloud systems, by anyone. A common DNS mistake can leave them open for attackers to grab, which can lead to credential theft and worse. We demonstrated the attack is still possible in 2026, including finding real takeovers on US treasury domains, which were reported and fixed via a bug bounty program.

The cost to us for doing this was just $3 per valid takeover - what a bargain! We only covered less than 1% of the total IP space, so there are many more out there for attackers to grab. So, now is the time to review your DNS records and get those dangling records squashed ASAP.

As of the time of writing, the attack still works in practice, and though there are some controls to ban attackers abusing the system, there are sufficient gaps to make the attack practical, and at a reasonable cost.

Quad9 disabled its recursive DNS service for users in France on Nov. 24, 2026, after French courts upheld demands from sports rightsholder beIn to block domains the company linked to alleged piracy streaming sites.

The nonprofit DNS provider said its servers will refuse queries from France reaching any Quad9 service address. Quad9 set the shutdown for 9 a.m. Central European Time, a window the organization chose to give affected users time to change their DNS settings during business hours, according to its blog post .
